idiom_name: enum with per-variant fields + exhaustive match + fallible constructors
implementation_notes: Rust's enum is the pattern's home: a value is exactly one of its variants, each variant carries only the fields that make sense for it, and match is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler, so a new variant is a compile error everywhere it is not handled. Make the fields private and expose fallible constructors (fn connect(..) -> Result<Connected, Error>, TryFrom) so the member invariants hold, and let Option/Result replace nullable-state pairs; deriving PartialEq, Debug and serde with an explicit tag keeps the variants visible at the wire boundary. The classic sealed-hierarchy structure has no reason to exist - the enum plus match replaces it entirely, and the compiler, not a convention, owns closure and exhaustiveness.
pitfalls: A catch-all arm (_ => ...) silently swallows every future variant: the compiler is satisfied and the guarantee disappears exactly when the model grows.

#[non_exhaustive] on a public enum forces downstream crates to add a wildcard arm, trading the compile-time guarantee for semver-compatible extension - add it deliberately, and handle the unknown case explicitly.

Deriving Default requires marking one variant #[default], and a default-constructed enum value is a legal but often meaningless state; prefer a constructor with parameters over Default for state machines.
